content:
@Christian Merten this is a great example where we can try to stress test your trust tool!

Minor feature request: I would love to (so to speak) open AlgebraicGeometry. Because currently almost all the nodes start with a handful of namespaces that don't really give any information to the reader.

I've been building a very similar tool, which I described at #AI authored projects > Referee in July. It also builds a website to explore the graph of dependencies (excluding proof dependencies) of a statement, and can also be built from a github action (see this repository). Its output for HodgeConjecture is https://remydegenne.github.io/HodgeConjecture/chapter-statement/module-statement/decl-HodgeConjecture/. Click on a node to see its card below the graph (and click on "everything it rests on" to see way too many cards).

@Christian Merten we should talk about it rather than building in parallel! I'll DM you.

Paul Lezeau said:

For people are are interested in helping out on the Hodge conjecture formalisation work, I’ll share a list of tasks that could be worked on shortly

Shared in new thread: #Formal conjectures > Coordination for the Hodge Conjecture formalisation

@Christian Merten @Rémy Degenne out of curiosity, is there any way to label a given definition in the tool as "trusted" (e.g. adding a @[trusted] attribute or something like that in the lean file)? The use case I had in mind would be for large formalisations (like this one), we could eventually work our way up the tree of dependencies and keep track of what has been been accepted versus what still needs to be checked.

Maybe rather than a plain @[trusted] tag in the code, it would be nice if "trustworthiness" were pinned to the precise declaration using a similar system as comparator. That way i.e. if the meaning of a statement is in inadvertently altered by an upstream code change, the difference can be automatically detected.

I think many people have built environment filtering for displaying trust. See eg mattrobball/lean-stan which sprang from mattrobball/lean-informal. It would be good to share lessons.

My goal is to support my laziness -- extract the challenge file, not write it. But the same principles apply. It doesn't really work at the moment because comparator descends into theorem bodies in the closure of the challenge file. And I just want to mark those as sorry.

For flagging trusted, the solution I had is human-review + tags + CI to detect changes in the closure. I think with the MI semantic diffs you can cut down the work. This was what I used back in March for bridgeland. I have not thought a better one.
I remember Remy already building this out more...

Paul Lezeau said:

Christian Merten Rémy Degenne out of curiosity, is there any way to label a given definition in the tool as "trusted" (e.g. adding a @[trusted] attribute or something like that in the lean file)? The use case I had in mind would be for large formalisations (like this one), we could eventually work our way up the tree of dependencies and keep track of what has been been accepted versus what still needs to be checked.

I don't know about Rémy's tool, but in the one I shared you can assert that you trust a given declaration through the web interface. You can also use the CLI to create a "trust certificate" and sign it with your PGP key. These certificates can then be published to any trust server. The certificates are tied to a given semantic hash.
For a trusted attribute, you could have something like @[trusted <hash>] where <hash> is the semantic hash of the declaration. A linter could then check if the <hash> agrees with the semantic hash.

What I dislike about a trusted declaration in the codebase is that it does not allow for declaring "Person X trusts this declaration". Trusting a declaration is a personal decision. You may decide that you consider some people as trustworthy and some not, so you may want to consider only declarations as trusted that someone that you trust has declared as "trusted".

In my website there is a "Your audit" window below the declaration cards, where you can click "accepted". The graph then shows a green tick for that declaration. The tool use semantic hashes to detect that something you accepted changed in a later version and invalidates the acceptation.
A difference with Christian's website is that I made that audit verdict personal and did not add sharing functionalities.
I think a good experiment is to compare expert judgement to just fable and astra arguing to agreement about NL/formal alignment. Either situation is expensive so should be stored.

Christian Merten said:

What I dislike about a trusted declaration in the codebase is that it does not allow for declaring "Person X trusts this declaration". Trusting a declaration is a personal decision. You may decide that you consider some people as trustworthy and some not

Absolutely, "trust" is a social problem, not a mathematical one.

What I'd really like is something like social media for proofs. I want to be able to "like"/"dislike" certain statements, follow my favorite mathematicians to see what they endorse, maybe join certain organizations like Mathlib Initiative, TauCeti, Formal Conjectures so that I can trust their code when I import it into my projects. trust-server I think is a strong step towards this.

Although this discussion is a bit off topic, and maybe is better for another thread specifically about building a good trust/auditing UI.
Yeah, I imagined some child of Youtube + PGP would come out of here.

An issue I have with these "trust" tools that compute a small graph of definitions that should be sufficient to understand the final result is that you have to trust that the tree generated is indeed sufficient.

You can see that the two websites linked above for HodgeConjecture don't show the same number of nodes. And it makes sense, since you can make many decisions differently: we don't show dependencies used in proofs of theorems, that's clear, but what about proofs of Prop-valued structure fields? Those are in the body of a def, so a tool that only prunes proofs of theorems would show them, but they can be omitted. So what about replacing all proofs everywhere by sorry? Well perhaps that's too radical because a def of the shape Exists.choose existence_theorem would become Exists.choose sorry. Hard to accept the meaning of that one in review. It's easy to make (or let your AI make) an "optimization" of your tree that could prune something that should not.

That's partly why on top of the dependency graph computation at MeaningGraph (that does several of these choices) I also wrote the challenge file generator at ChallengeGen. It has two modes:
(a) a Lean file generator that tries to produce readable Lean files by copying from the source. It has to deal with namespaces and open statements and all of that is complex and compilation is not 100% guaranteed even if the list of dependencies is sufficient. That's the same idea as what Matt was doing. I just saw that on HodgeConjecture it's missing many noncomputable (perhaps because of a noncomputable section, that never showed up in my tests?) and a few open.
(b) a second generator that renders each declaration from their ConstantInfo and gives a file that is completely unreadable. But that one should absolutely compile. If it does not, the dependency list is wrong and something was pruned that should not have been.

The generator (b) is in my mind essential to be able to trust the meaning graph tool. It tests that the extracted dependency trees are sufficient to lead to the desired theorem. It does not tell you if your tree is minimal, and it cannot catch the Exists.choose sorry issue though.

Ideally I would check the compilation of the files generated by (b) when creating the website but that's very slow to do for all declarations of a project so I'm currently not doing it. I did some test of MeaningGraph versus all declarations from a few libraries some time back to check that it was good, but that occasional test against other libraries is not a solid enough trust argument for the graph generated on a new project.
I guess when building the website I could test the few files of the main theorems of the library and not the others, that could be fast enough.

I had to repeatedly remind models that lean syntax is more complex than they think.

So what about replacing all proofs everywhere by sorry? Well perhaps that's too radical because a def of the shape Exists.choose existence_theorem would become Exists.choose sorry

I would be kinda terrified if the someone or something did not factor out the proof of a nontrivial existence statement. And I would set the boundaries at not pruning named constants.

There has to be better a solution than running for all declarations!
